assumptions: Adequacy against a REGISTERED fault model is not completeness. Nothing here establishes that the fault model contains every fault this semantics can have.

Equivalence is decidable HERE because the domain is finite — 9 edges × 32 inputs plus every single-kind closure is the complete extensional signature. That is a property of this size, not of the method.
attrs.evidence: 12 registered mutants, 0 survivors. M1–M8 are GPT-5.6’s, named in its R7.4 audit; M3b, M4b, M9–M11 are this round’s, and M9/M10 exist BECAUSE RUNNING GPT-5.6’S OWN FAULT MODEL AGAINST THE R7.4 TREE FOUND FOUR SURVIVORS. M3 and its mirror survived because operational()’s two guards were never separated by any edge. M9 survived because the declared-additive fold was reached only inside §6’s negative control, where every rule maps to ∅ — so `union the consequents` and `return ∅` were the same function. M10 survived and is UNSOUND: it reports `nothing affected` for an impact nobody classified. E7, E8 and E9 were added to discriminate them. THE KILL CRITERION IS A DIFFERENCE FROM THE REFERENCE, not a red check: §3 shows M3 failing zero battery rows and being killed only because promoting an edge to operational DELETED that edge’s UNKNOWN-TOP row. Equivalence is decided by extensional signature comparison over the finite domain, which removes the equivalent-mutant problem at this size instead of arguing about it.

attrs.review_focus: The uncomfortable number is FOUR: GPT-5.6 proposed this fault model in the same audit that found the monotonicity hole, and running it against the tree it was auditing killed four more things than the audit named. A fault model is worth more than the finding that produced it.
attrs.statement: Every mutant in the registered fault model for the impact semantics is killed by a stated observation, and mutant equivalence is decided rather than asserted.
